name: Google Kubernetes Engine
summary: Google’s managed Kubernetes, the oldest one: Google runs the control plane, and in Autopilot mode the nodes too.
intro: In GKE, Google runs each cluster’s control plane: the Kubernetes API server, the scheduler, the controllers and the database that holds cluster state. That database is etcd running on the control plane VMs, or Google’s Spanner, but every cluster serves the etcd API, so the Kubernetes API server talks to both the same way. A zonal cluster has its control plane in one zone; a regional cluster keeps replicas in several zones, so it stays reachable through a zone outage and during upgrades. Google upgrades the control plane on a schedule set by the release channel you pick: Rapid, Regular (the default), Stable or Extended.

GKE has two modes. In Standard mode you design node pools, groups of Compute Engine VMs with a machine type you choose, and pay for those VMs whether Pods fill them or not. In Autopilot mode, launched in 2021 and now Google’s recommendation, Google creates, sizes, patches and repairs the nodes, and for general-purpose Pods you pay per second for the CPU, memory and storage each Pod requests. Since 2025 a Standard cluster can also run selected workloads in Autopilot mode. For untrusted code, GKE Sandbox runs a Pod inside gVisor, a user-space kernel that answers most system calls itself, or, on recent versions, inside its own microVM using Kata Containers.
strengths: Autopilot’s per-Pod billing means you don’t pay for half-empty nodes on general-purpose workloads
The free tier credits one zonal or Autopilot cluster’s fee each month per billing account
Very large clusters: Google announced support for 65,000 nodes in November 2024
Built-in sandboxing with gVisor or microVMs for multi-tenant or untrusted workloads
limits: A flat $0.10 per cluster per hour, rising to $0.60 while a cluster on the Extended channel sits in extended support
Autopilot gives up node access: no SSH to the VMs, and Pods must fit its security and configuration constraints (privileged Pods need Standard)
The free tier doesn’t cover regional Standard clusters, and the zonal control plane SLA is only 99.5%
Clusters are upgraded automatically; maintenance windows and exclusions shape the timing, but staying on one minor version for long needs the paid Extended channel

sections.title: What a cluster costs (checked 2026-10-06)
sections.intro: Every cluster pays the same management fee whatever its size or mode. Compute is billed on top: per node in Standard, per Pod request in Autopilot.

rows.label: Cluster management fee
values: Billed per second; same for zonal, regional and Autopilot

rows.label: Free tier
values: Per billing account; zonal and Autopilot clusters only

rows.label: Extended support period
values: Extended channel only, up to 24 months on one minor version

rows.label: Standard compute
values: You pay for every node in your node pools

rows.label: Autopilot compute
values: CPU, memory and ephemeral storage; node-based pricing plus a premium for specific hardware

notes: From the GKE pricing page, checked on 2026-10-06. The control plane SLA is 99.95% for Autopilot and regional clusters and 99.5% for zonal clusters.

story: Google ran its own services in containers on an internal cluster manager called Borg for about a decade before Kubernetes. After open-sourcing Kubernetes in June 2014, it wanted Google Cloud customers to be able to use it without running it themselves. On November 4, 2014 it announced an alpha of Google Container Engine, a managed cluster manager for Docker containers built on Kubernetes. The name started with C, but Google used the acronym GKE from the start “in a nod to Kubernetes”.

Container Engine left beta and became generally available on August 26, 2015. In November 2017, after joining the CNCF’s Certified Kubernetes program, Google renamed it Google Kubernetes Engine. Around the same time it dropped its cluster management fee, which had been $0.15 per hour for clusters of six or more nodes; in June 2020 it brought back a flat $0.10 per hour together with a financially backed SLA.

In February 2021 Google launched Autopilot, a second mode where Google also runs the nodes and bills by Pod. It has since become the default recommendation, and in 2025 Google started letting Standard clusters run Autopilot workloads too. Scale kept growing with AI training: GKE announced support for 65,000-node clusters in November 2024. In September 2025 Google moved GKE to a single paid tier that includes multi-cluster features such as Fleets, Config Management and Policy Controller at no extra cost.

choices.choice: Run upstream Kubernetes, not a Borg service
choices.why: Google wanted customers to run the same open-source system anywhere. GKE runs certified Kubernetes, and Google says it puts the improvements needed for scale, such as those behind 65,000-node clusters, into open-source Kubernetes.

Some teams want full control of node pools and machine types; others find that much choice “overwhelming or unnecessary”. Autopilot lets Google own the nodes and charge per Pod, while Standard stays for teams that need the control.

choices.choice: Serve the etcd API whatever the backing store
choices.why: Kubernetes expects etcd. Exposing the etcd API on every control plane lets Google back some clusters with Spanner instead, without changing Kubernetes itself.

choices.choice: A user-space kernel for untrusted Pods
choices.why: Containers share the host kernel, so a kernel bug can let one tenant escape. GKE Sandbox puts gVisor between the Pod and the host kernel without changing the application.
